rationale: I'm replacing raw Pearson correlations with a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf shrunk correlation matrices, using the CC200 atlas without global signal regression. The reference point is the log-Euclidean mean of the training fold only. Abraham et al. (2017) found tangent-space features the most reliable connectivity measure for ABIDE classification across sites. Projecting each subject's matrix relative to the group mean respects the geometry of these matrices and removes shared structure, which can make the autism-related differences easier for a linear classifier to separate. The Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage also keeps matrices from subjects with all-zero ROIs valid (positive definite).

I'm replacing the single CC200 model with an ensemble over four parcellations: CC200, CC400, AAL and Harvard-Oxford. Each atlas gets the same tangent-space plus L2 logistic regression pipeline, and the final prediction averages their scores after scaling each atlas's scores by their spread on the training data. Different parcellations capture the same connectome at different resolutions and boundaries, so their errors should partly cancel. Abraham et al. (2017) and later ABIDE multi-atlas work found that combining atlases is more robust across sites than any single atlas.

I'm adding site harmonization on the matrix manifold, a Riemannian re-centering (Zanini et al. 2018). Each subject's matrix is now projected relative to the log-Euclidean mean of its own site, instead of one global training mean. ABIDE's site differences in scanner, TR and protocol are large, and re-centering each site at the identity removes those site shifts while keeping the within-site connectivity differences that separate autism from controls. The site means use only label-free information: the subjects' matrices and the site covariate, pooled over training and test subjects of that site.

After each site is re-centred, sites still differ in how spread out their tangent vectors are. Scans with a shorter duration or a different TR give noisier connectivity estimates, so those sites scatter more widely around the identity. I'll add the "stretching" step of Riemannian Procrustes analysis (Rodrigues et al. 2019): each site's re-centred tangent vectors are divided by that site's root-mean-square norm. This equalises spread across sites using only the matrices and the site covariate, with no labels. The goal is that high-noise sites stop dominating the shared linear classifier.

I'm adding three more views to the ensemble: CC200, AAL and HO computed with global signal regression (`filt_global`). Each goes through the same pipeline (site re-centring, stretching, tangent space, logistic regression) and is averaged with the four existing no-GSR atlases. GSR removes the global fluctuations that are largely driven by breathing, heart rate and motion and that differ by site. This gives a different view of the connectome with partly independent errors, so averaging should help. CC400 is left out of the GSR set to keep memory and run time within the limit.

I'll regress out the effect of age and sex from each standardized tangent feature. ABIDE spans ages 7 to 64, and development and sex change connectivity strongly, so this variance is noise for diagnosis. The covariates are centred within each site, so they match the site-recentred features. The age and sex slopes are fitted on training subjects only, using covariates and features with no labels, and then applied to train and test.

The current logistic regression strength C is a fixed guess. I'll choose it for each atlas with inner grouped CV on the training fold over a grid of 0.1× to 10× the current value, using `groups_train`. To keep this cheap and exact, each L2 model is fitted on its SVD row-space coordinates. By the representer theorem, an n×n model gives the same solution as one on all ~20k–77k features. Atlases differ a lot in resolution and noise, so one hand-set penalty is probably not the right bias–variance trade-off for all of them.

I'm replacing the per-ROI z-scored correlation matrices with Ledoit-Wolf covariance matrices. Each subject's time series is scaled by one global factor, the RMS of their non-zero ROI standard deviations. This keeps the relative regional amplitude, a proxy for ALFF that differs in autism, inside the tangent-space embedding. It also removes arbitrary scanner and subject intensity scale. Remaining site-level amplitude shifts are handled by the existing per-site re-centering and stretching.

After per-site re-centring and stretching, the tangent vectors sit in a common space where the Riemannian metric already weights all connections equally (no direction is preferred). The current per-feature StandardScaler breaks that. It inflates low-variance, mostly noise connections to the same weight as the informative high-variance ones before the strongly regularized logistic regression. I'll replace it with training-mean centring plus one global scale factor, chosen so the average feature variance is 1 as before. This keeps the existing C on the same footing while restoring the geometry the Riemannian methods rely on.

I'm adding the Dosenbach-160 atlas as a fifth view, run through the same pipeline: shrunk correlation, per-site re-centring and stretching, tangent space, then logistic regression. The four current atlases are all anatomical or data-driven tilings of the whole cortex. Dosenbach-160 is a functionally defined set of 10-mm spheres from a meta-analysis, organised into default-mode, cingulo-opercular/salience, fronto-parietal, sensorimotor, occipital and cerebellar networks. Those networks are the ones implicated in autism, and because the parcellation samples them so differently, its errors should be less correlated with the other four, which should help the averaged ensemble.

Re-centring each site on its own mean removes the scanner shift, but it also removes each site's diagnostic base rate. The CV folds are grouped by subject, so sites are shared between train and test. I'll put that information back as an empirical-Bayes site prior: each site's training autism rate, shrunk toward the global rate with 20 pseudo-subjects, is added in log-odds to the ensemble score. The score is first converted to log-odds by assuming two equal-variance Gaussian classes with AUC ≈ 0.78, which multiplies the test-standardized score by 1.24. A site not seen in training gets a prior of zero.

Within-subject noise in connectivity estimates is large, and the strongly regularized linear model cannot tell reliable edge differences from noisy ones. As a noise-aware regularizer, I'll add split-half augmentation for training. Each training subject also contributes connectivity matrices from the first and second halves of its scan, with the same label and sample weights that sum to 1 per subject. This pushes the classifier toward directions that stay stable within a subject. Each half-scan version gets its own per-site re-centering and stretching, because shorter scans are noisier and more shrunk. To stay inside the time limit this only applies to the atlases with 250 ROIs or fewer (CC200, AAL, HO). CC400 and test-time scoring use only the full-scan matrices, as before.

The classifier already learns from split-half matrices in training, so I'll reuse them at test time. Each subject's score becomes the 0.5/0.25/0.25 weighted average of its full-scan, first-half and second-half decision values, matching the training weights. Within-subject noise is large, so averaging over sub-scan views should lower the variance of each test subject's score. This is nearly free, because the half-scan site re-centring is already computed for test subjects and was being thrown away. The averaged score is standardized with the same averaging applied to the training subjects, so atlases stay on a comparable scale.

Split-half augmentation and test-time averaging have both helped, so I'm adding a third half-length window: the middle half of the scan (T/4 to 3T/4). It overlaps both existing halves, adding one more within-subject view of the connectivity matrix for the three smaller atlases. It is used in training and at test time, with weights 0.5 for the full scan and 1/6 for each half-window. More sub-scan views should further reduce the effect of within-subject noise on the classifier and on each test subject's score.

Split-half augmentation in training, then reused at test time, gave the two most recent gains, but only CC400 was left out, for compute reasons. This change applies the same first-half/second-half views, with their own per-site re-centring and stretching, to CC400 as well. That makes the noise-aware regularization cover all four ensemble members. To stay within memory, the tangent views are now kept in float32 and the classifier's design matrix is built once in float64.

Re-centring each site on the mean of all its subjects is biased when a site's diagnosis mix is unbalanced, because the reference shifts toward the majority class. In a site that is 70% autism, the autism subjects end up looking less autistic, which blurs the training signal and gives each site a different offset in the pooled score. I'll correct each site's log-Euclidean reference to a class-balanced one: reference = all-subject mean + (mean of the two training class means − unweighted training mean). This is like ComBat with the diagnosis covariate protected. It uses only training-fold labels, still uses test subjects' matrices (no labels) for precision, and falls back to the old reference when a site has fewer than 3 training subjects in either class.

Head motion is the main source of artifactual connectivity in ABIDE, and high-motion subjects give noisy, biased matrices that the shared classifier currently treats the same as clean ones. I'll down-weight them in training with a soft quality weight w = 1/(1+(mean_fd/0.3)^2), normalized to mean 1 within each class so class balance and the effective C are unchanged. This uses only the non-label covariate, never removes features, and doesn't change how test subjects are scored.
